📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remember when Olivia Wilde was served child custody papers by Jason Sudeikis while she was on stage in front of thousands presenting Don’t Worry Darling at CinemaCon? That was over four years ago in the heat of the pair figuring out the post-split situation. However, these days, the two seem to be on better terms. To that point, Sudeikis is even crediting his ex for the creation of his massively successful TV show, Ted Lasso (which just got major news by the way).

Sudeikis recently said two very notable things about his high-profile breakup. One of those came up when he was on Talk Easy with Sam Fragoso, during which he said his and Wilde's split was “more complicated” and “more human” than how it was portrayed in the media. And on another occasion, Sudeikis went out of his way to talk about how Wilde played a role in getting Ted Lasso made. In his words to the Smartless podcast:.

I remember Olivia and I were out to dinner and she's like, 'What are you guys gonna do with that? Like, you guys love doing that thing so much. You should do something with that.' I was like, ‘Yeah.’ And then, her and I just started chatting about it at dinner a little bit like, ‘That would be fun.’.

As Sudeikis shared during an interview at a special live edition of the show at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles, Wilde was the person who actually followed up with her then-partner on the Ted Lasso idea years before him and the other creators knew what to do with the character. As Sudeikis continued:.

Industry observers note that then Joe and Brendan come out to New York and we hang out for a week in Brooklyn... And then for three days straight, we just start filling up pages of ideas and realize, ‘Oh, this might be a TV show.’ And then we didn't do anything with it for three years.

Wild, right? Mr. Ted Lasso himself, alongside two of his co-creators Brendan Hunt, Joe Kelly, sat on the idea for a while until one day they were overflowing with ideas. And then, they sat on it again until this happened. In Sudeikis’ words:.

It wasn’t until Bill Lawrence came to me with an idea for another TV show that I was like ‘Ah, this isn’t the right fit.’ He goes, ‘Well, if you have any ideas…’ I go, ‘Well, here’s a stack of papers of stuff we wrote down.’ And he read it, and was like, ‘Oh yeah, there’s definitely a show here.’.

Now that Ted Lasso is one of the best shows to watch with an Apple TV subscription, it’s pretty crazy to think how long the whole process took. It took so long that when the idea was first formed Sudeikis and Wilde went from being an engaged couple to splitting up. Thankfully it did, because it’s one of my favorite shows on streaming in recent years.

Recent findings suggest that and did you know there’s even a tribute to Olivia Wilde in Ted Lasso? The AFC Richmond locker room (at one point at least) features Wilde’s actual surname, “Cockburn,” alongside the names of other writers’ friends, family members and former mentors within the production.

Industry observers note that over the past summer, Olivia Wilde spoke a bit to her divorce as well, sharing the conversation that led to their split. Wilde is also having a massive year herself, thanks to her latest directorial effort, The Invite, and Sudeikis says he’s “thrilled” for her success. As for him, he just got some good news, as Ted Lasso was just officially renewed for Season 5 by Apple. So the show remains the gift that keeps on giving. In short, thank you, Jason and Olivia!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that players who abused World of Warcraft: Forever's Blackmaw Hold unintended gold farm, which allowed a small minority of players to hoard thousands of gold in a few days, have drawn the ire of WoW publisher, Blizzard.
  • Recent findings suggest that for those unaware, the World of Warcraft: Forever community was greatly alarmed by this gold farm, which had players clear the same non-elite enemies from the new late game dungeon, Blackmaw Hold.
  • There was much speculation on what would happen to those who participated in this exploit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that players who abused World of Warcraft: Forever's Blackmaw Hold unintended gold farm, which allowed a small minority of players to hoard thousands of gold in a few days, have drawn the ire of WoW publisher, Blizzard. Suspensions have been issued, trade locks have been put on accounts, and ill-gotten gold is being seized.

Recent findings suggest that for those unaware, the World of Warcraft: Forever community was greatly alarmed by this gold farm, which had players clear the same non-elite enemies from the new late game dungeon, Blackmaw Hold. By quickly clearing select mobs with area-of-effect damage, players would loot upwards of 100 raw gold an hour. This exploit, clearly not intentional, was nonetheless farmed until Blizzard hotfixed it earlier in the week.

There was much speculation on what would happen to those who participated in this exploit. That speculation would come to an end late last night with an official statement from the World of Warcraft: Forever development team.

"As players continue their journey into WoW Forever’s higher-level content, we are closely monitoring the game economy to ensure that gold sources and costs are well balanced," the statement reads. "Finding efficient farming spots has always been part of the game, and is how most players have earned their epic mounts since 2004. When a single location proves so lucrative that it overshadows all other sources, we generally adjust it to bring it in line with the rest.".

It goes on to explain the nature of the bug that made this gold farm possible, before reassuring those who may have accidentally benefited from some extra cash from their regular runs of Blackmaw Hold they have nothing to worry about. The same cannot be said for those who took advantage of the situation.

In a recent development, "Players who simply ran Blackmaw Hold a few times and benefited organically from the extra loot did nothing wrong, and no one should worry that they’re putting their account at risk if they accidentally benefit from a bug," it continues. "But there were a couple hundred players worldwide who recognized that this was unintended and spent significant time exclusively farming that group of enemies.

"Yesterday, we put an economy lock on their accounts to prevent broader impact to the game economy while we investigated the extent of the exploitative gains, including gold earned by vendoring bugged drops. Today, we are in the process of removing all such gold earned, as well as applying account suspensions to significant abusers.".

The post concludes by thanking players for their feedback on the matter, and a final warning: "As always, we advise all players to refrain from abusing game mechanics that are clearly unintended. We will continue to take action against intentional abuse.".

This decision certainly sets the precedent moving forward with World of Warcraft: Forever that such exploits won't be tolerated, and rolling back the wealth of those who made out of Blackmaw Hold like bandits is a good measure that should prevent continuous damage.

It has been revealed that inevitably the exploit would have had some impact, specifically in those days prior to trading blocks being put in place. While the gold on the exploiter's accounts may be removed, any purchases they made on the in-game auction house will have affected others through buying and selling goods with ample funds.

Those who were suspended temporarily will be able to regain access to the game by the time the first wave of raids come out in December, so it very much feels like a firm slap on the wrist in that regard. Even so, given the establishment of punishments for such behavior, one can only wonder if future events will come with harsher penalties.

Industry observers note that world of Warcraft: Forever, despite this small economic roadbump, is proving exceptionally popular for Blizzard. It's already broken records for the series, and has impressed players so far with its revamping of the classic MMO.

Forgotten car combat game Destruction AllStars has been in some stage of extinction for years now, but if you do have the PS5 game in your library, then today truly is the last day you can play it in any meaningful manner.

From tomorrow, 25th November 2026, the last of its game services will be taken offline.

The multiplayer servers were already permanently pulled in May 2026, and within the next 24 hours, "all remaining game services will be taken offline", per communication from Sony.

Single player modes had still been available to play, but those will be removed too when their servers are taken offline.

Quite literally the only content left in Destruction AllStars after tomorrow is an arcade mode and challenges. Even then, though, Sony warns the "functionality and player experience" tied to that content could be impacted.

Basically, if you want to experience even a sliver of the Destruction AllStars experience, you've only got today left to do it. It's already been delisted from the PS Store, so if you don't have a copy now, you're completely out of luck.

It's not like you'd be missing out on much, to be fair.

Sources indicate that destruction AllStars never made a splash in terms of quality or popularity. While it did have a small playerbase during its days with active servers, the game promptly died out after a February 2021 release.

Will you be playing Destruction AllStars one last time today? Let us know in the comments below.

In a recent development, I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

It has been revealed that show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Sources indicate that per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

In Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

Sources indicate that the fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

Industry observers note that is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the weekend, there was a whole lot of buzz amongst the GTA 6 community about a Quick Resume glitch that unlocks the game's frame rate on Xbox Series X and S, potentially allowing it to reach 60FPS and higher.
  • Industry observers note that follow-up tests highlighted that the results were averaging more around the 30-35FPS range consistently, and some of the game's animations appeared to be running at double speed.
  • Rich Leadbetter of DF found that he reached an average of 36FPS on Xbox Series X in the first hour of the game:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the weekend, there was a whole lot of buzz amongst the GTA 6 community about a Quick Resume glitch that unlocks the game's frame rate on Xbox Series X and S, potentially allowing it to reach 60FPS and higher.

Industry observers note that follow-up tests highlighted that the results were averaging more around the 30-35FPS range consistently, and some of the game's animations appeared to be running at double speed. The experts at Digital Foundry have now weighed in on this, and they've come to pretty much the same conclusion - that it's not really a viable way to play.

Rich Leadbetter of DF found that he reached an average of 36FPS on Xbox Series X in the first hour of the game:.

Sources indicate that "Unfortunately, while the unlock glitch is academically interesting, it doesn't provide a huge improvement to responsiveness. Our capture tools show frame-rates in the 30fps to 40fps range on Series X, with Rich recording an average frame-rate of 36fps during the first hour of the game.".

The sped-up gameplay is also mentioned, described as an "oddity" that "makes the game inconsistent and harder to control", although this is stated to be more likely a result of the bug rather than GTA 6's code being tied to frame rate.

Nevertheless, there's one specific advantage that's brought up as part of this glitch, which is that it reduces the game's input lag. Digital Foundry's tests highlighted that the game provided around 170ms of lag at the 30FPS mark, while a 40FPS scene dropped it to around 120ms. However, the varied frame rates are said to provide an "unsettling" feel overall, and one that probably outweighs the smoother feel during specific 30FPS+ moments.

The outlet indicates that a 40FPS mode when using a VRR supported display "could still make sense" on Xbox Series X, but "the game's CPU limits remain the largest barrier against such a mode" due to occasions where GTA 6 can't even reach 30FPS as things stand, while it might also require extra work such as implementing FSR upscaling tech.

"A 40fps mode with VRR could still make sense, but it's far from an open-and-shut case to say that such a mode would be an improvement overall against the current 30fps cap. It might also require extra work, such as integrated FSR 4 on Series X in service of a higher frame-rate when GPU limited, which wouldn't be the work of a moment. Finally, it looks like a 60fps mode is fundamentally unachievable on current console hardware.".

Recent findings suggest that who knows whether Rockstar Games will be able to put in the work to provide a 40FPS mode in the future, but we're going to bet they'll stick with 30FPS and simply aim for 60FPS when Xbox Project Helix and the PS6 hit the market. They've got plenty of work to do with the PC version of GTA 6, not to mention the GTA Online version of the game that's surely in the works, so pushing to hit 40FPS on current-gen consoles seems unlikely.

What are your thoughts on this? Let us know down in the comments section below.

Stealing the Schafter V12 in GTA 6 is one of the car theft missions you'll have to complete to gain Raul's trust, but similar to the BF Bandito or Declasse Vamos, it's a little tricky. Make sure to grab the silenced pistol from the trunk of the car outside—not necessarily because you'll need it, but because it's a handy weapon to have.

According to recent reports, now, as you can see in the video above, you can get into the chop shop by climbing up the van around back and then onto the roof. I'd then suggest dropping down on the right side, where there are few enemies, knocking out the guy sitting by the gate, then opening it by hitting the left button.

Sneak back towards the centre of the chop shop and turn left to find the Declasse Vamos, a black unassuming car. Hop inside, start it up, and drive out of the gate you just opened. Easy, right? Now simply bring it to Randy's garage as directed. You also kill everyone inside if you wish, but my way above will get you that non-lethal Criminal Profile rating.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New Zealand's tourism board has taken advantage of all the excitement surrounding Grand Theft Auto 6's launch, as hordes of players who've changed their Xbox timezones to that of the world's second best rugby team (sorry) to jump into the game early.

"One perk of seeing the sun first? Getting GTA 6 first too," reads a post on the New Zealand tourist board's Instagram account: PureNewZealand. "We heard a few of you are trying the New Zealand trick to join us. We get it, and we'd love to have you." The post also includes a video of folks looking at all the natural beauty of New Zealand, presumably before they all look themselves indoors to play the video game, alongside the caption: "life, because we're getting GTA 6 first.".

According to recent reports, for those unaware, Xbox owners have been swapping their console time zones for years to New Zealand in order to take advantage of the region's access to games before anywhere else in the world. When games have, let's say, a worldwide release time of midnight across all nations, those living in New Zealand are able to jump in first as a result.

Microsoft has for years been happy to let this practice continue on its platform, and as such a sort of cultural norm about hopping on a digital plane for a game's release has been established. If you want guidance, we have a guide on how to pull off the GTA 6 Fresh Zealand trick yourself which can walk you through it.

If you aren't keen on doing so for whatever reason, you can find a breakdown of all the global launch times for GTA 6 too. If you want one final run through on what to expect from Rockstar's big release last minute, our Everything We Know about Grand Theft Auto 6 page should set you right for good measure.

  • I don't play video games regularly anymore.
  • According to recent reports, here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019.
  • My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a newly introduced legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

According to recent reports, here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my newly introduced parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. Fresh players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

According to recent reports, what I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

Recent findings suggest that as time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

Sources indicate that the original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as significant as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

Industry observers note that I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an vital byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

Industry observers note that the changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn newly introduced tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

In a recent development, as the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a upcoming mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted prepares designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

In a recent development, for players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

Industry News: Slay the Spire 2 is one of this year's best selling games despite only being available on PC, and its players are "obsessed"

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One million copies for each month on sale, it seems.
  • That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.
  • In a recent development, slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One million copies for each month on sale, it seems. Slay the Spire 2, Mega Crit's roguelike deckbuilder, is estimated to have sold 7.9m copies since its release in Steam Early Access in March.

That's according to estimates by Alinea Analytics industry analyst Rhys Elliott, who revealed in a LinkedIn post that those sales translate to $157.6m (~£119.6m) in revenue for the small studio.

In a recent development, slay the Spire 2 is now the sixth best-selling 2026 release across Steam, PlayStation and Xbox. That is notable, as the game is only out on Steam, meaning it has sold enough copies to outpace games on platforms it's not even available on.

It has been revealed that we already knew Slay the Spire 2 was one of the year's biggest releases. In its first week on sale, the game sold over 3m copies. It quickly became March's top-selling game on Steam, beating blockbuster competition in Crimson Desert and Resident Evil Requiem. Slay the Spire 2, alongside other indie titles such as Meccha Chameleon, have helped Steam deliver another record year of revenue.

Sources indicate that it was such a hit, even, that other indie developers felt it negatively impacted sales of their own games. Mewgenics maker Edmund McMillen recently told Eurogamer "it sucked everybody out". "The same players who liked Mewgenics, they were Slay The Spire players. So they all went woosh and right over," McMillen said.

Slay the Spire 2 has been consistently popular with players, too, and that popularity has seemingly continued. Elliott noted the game never fell below 2.5 million active players each month since March.

According to recent reports, slay the Spire 2's loyal following also meant that the recently released beta patch, which added a new character, was enough to bring back millions of players. Despite only being available for players who opt into the beta branch of the game, Slay the Spire 2 more than doubled its daily active customers to reach its highest daily player count in six months.

Industry observers note that "Simply put: Slay the Spire 2 players are obsessed," wrote Elliott. "And it's not just a niche group of dedicated players, either. The average play time is nearly 84 hours, sure. But zooming out, 1.9 million folks have played for over 100 hours.".

Incidentally, nearly 100,000 players bought the game but never played it, which Elliott added could explain the discrepancy between player numbers and copies sold.

Looking ahead, Slay the Spire 2's road to version 1.0 is expected to be long, with several features and gameplay additions still in the works. Then there are the console ports, which have yet to be confirmed, but are very much expected.

In Eurogamer's Slay the Spire 2 early access review, Bertie Purchese called it "a deceptively familiar sequel" whose confident design and smart upcoming additions build on what made the original work so well.

If you were a tween or teen in the late '90s and early 2000s, then you probably had or knew someone who had a crush on Chad Michael Murray. While he first won over the hearts of millions as the teen heartthrob in the hit teen drama One Tree Hill and the beloved teen rom-com A Cinderella Story, Murray has continued to make audiences swoon over him in a plethora of romance movies, including a steady stream of Christmas-themed ones. I was bummed when I didn’t see his name in any of the upcoming Netflix releases or in Hallmark's Countdown to Christmas lineup, but it turns out Murray is in a new Christmas movie, and it’s streaming right now.

It won’t be a Murray-less Christmas after all! The former teen heartthrob stars in Postcards for Christmas, which is available to anyone with an active Hulu subscription. The holiday flick centers on Hannah (Jessica Lowndes), who has traveled to Mistletoe Valley to temporarily help her college best friend run the local post office. When Hannah discovers a batch of love letter postcards that were never delivered, she becomes determined to reunite the star-crossed lovers. She teams up with Ford (Murray), the local radio DJ, and the pair read a postcard every day leading up to Christmas as they try to solve the mystery of who these letters could belong to.

I happened to stumble on the film while scrolling through Hulu looking for something latest to watch and knew I had to check it out. I’m so glad I did because Postcards for Christmas did not disappoint. Both Murray and Lowndes were great on screen together, and I really enjoyed the mystery angle of the romcom. It’s totally worth checking out, especially if you’re a fan of Murray.

I Just Found Out Chad Michael Murray Nearly Played A Different Character On One Tree Hill.

In a recent development, I should have known to check on Hulu’s holiday slate earlier, considering they’re really stepping up in the Christmas movie department lately, giving fans a latest place to check out holiday films outside of Netflix and Hallmark. It makes sense for Murray to appear on the streamer, considering it’s the current home to all nine seasons of One Tree Hill and several of his other romcoms, including last year’s holiday film Joy to the World.

It’s too early to say for sure, but it sounds like Murray might become Hulu’s go-to romantic lead for its Christmas flicks the same way Hallmark has been dominated by Lacey Chabert. I’m definitely not complaining!

Sources indicate that after watching Postcards for Christmas and Joy to World, Murray fans should head over to Netflix to catch him in the 2024 film The Merry Gentlemen, which the internet had a field day with. The current Sullivan’s Crossing star also appears in holiday films on Lifetime, Great American Family, and Hallmark.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as quickly as [she] possibly can".

Sources indicate that that's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having said following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as quickly as I possibly can.".

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

Sources indicate that to recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a upcoming organization Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the substantial game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, it was revealed that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead narrative designer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, won a BAFTA Breakthrough US award for her contribution to the hit 2025 game, which made history after winning 12 Game Award nominations last year. In the aftermath of her win, Svedberg-Yen dropped a pretty massive bombshell: she's no longer with the game's developer, Sandfall Interactive.

Industry observers note that "No, I left Sandfall in July, after wrapping up some final stuff for Expedition," she told Gamesbeat when asked if she's still with the company. "We've parted ways." As to what Svedberg-Yen is doing next, she offered a cryptic answer, including talk of writing "my own projects, my own stories". She also discussed another project she's set her sights on: establishing a fund to help mentor and grow a new generation of video game narrative designers.

In a recent development, "One of the initiatives I want to build is a narrative investment fund to focus on narrative-focused game creators, trying to bridge the gap between the seed stage and going to publishers," she explained, noting her background working in finance and how that dovetails nicely with her more recent experience as a narrative lead. "This is the chicken and egg question a lot of people face. To get money from publishers you need a demo, but to make a demo you need money. To get money you have to go to publishers. That’s an area where I would like to help a lot of these smaller creatives to get that seed funding so they can, in a way, de-risk themselves in the eyes of bigger investors.".

Her motivation for this initiative? Simply, she wants to change how the industry works. "I've discovered that quite a lot of studios don’t really know how to think about narrative, or how to integrate it into their pipelines and their processes. They tend to think it's a very narrow thing, when in fact it can influence all aspects. Part of this would also be an incubation program to help these studios develop those narrative foundations.".

According to recent reports, "The strongest feeling in me right now for 2027 is I want to help," she added later. "That sounds so cheesy and idealistic. I always cringe at myself for saying it. But I don't know how else to say it and be truthful. I want to help in some way, help the industry.".

Sandfall Interactive previously said its guiding "North Star" will always be its "own personal taste", and what the team enjoys.She noted that she didn't think the studio would bow to pressure from fans to do more of the same, but instead be guided by what it thinks is best for itself, and for the series. "I've seen too many TV reveals and books be swayed trying to please a lot of people, and in the process you end up losing the heart of what's there," she noted.

We know that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is "not the end" of the franchise, and it seems that whatever happens next, it'll have at least a little bit of Svedberg-Yen's creativity instilled in it. I wish her the best for whatever her next step is.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Someone, I won't name them just so I don't get them in trouble, once mentioned that EA doesn't shoot you, it puts a gun on the table and then comes in everyday and asks you if you'll shoot yourself, and they just keep coming in over and over until eventually you just are like 'Ugh, fine. Just stop bugging me about it, I'll do it.' And so the reality is that EA can legitimately say 'we didn't make BioWare do this, they chose to do this', but if you dig underneath that statement the reality is that the options on the table were all terrible. We chose the least terrible of the options." Via an interview with Pembridge.

Last month we got the devastating news that BioWare, the legendary studio that brought us Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and classics like Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, and the OG Baldur's Gate was being shut down. The decision was made by EA, just a year after it was acquired by a consortium made up of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and investment firms Silver Lake and Affinity Partners (owned by the son-in-law of US president Donald Trump, Jared Kushner).

The reasons? Underperforming games. Dragon Age: The Veilguard didn't hit the mark, Andromeda wasn't well received, and Anthem, the live-service shooter, shut its servers down for good earlier this year.

It's a bad string of events for sure, but former Dragon Age boss Mark Darrah doesn't believe that it's all down to BioWare's poor management. The studio was backed into a corner by EA and the pressure to perform.

Decisions like using the Frostbite Engine, "making Dragon Age 2", and "shipping Anthem" were all products of BioWare needing to hit financial targets set out by EA. "They basically said 'Gotta hit your financials, so what are you going to do?' Darrah says. "'Are you going to ship KOTOR a year sooner than you think is going to happen? No. Are you going to pull Mass Effect in a year? No. It was never clear what the consequence of 'no' was, and it still isn't. But it seemed really dire at the time. So you gotta do something, so what are you going to do? Did they make us make Dragon Age 2? No. But they made us do something.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the company created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt.
  • Recent findings suggest that this came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back.
  • Industry observers note that "Prior to the Firm's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, beleaguered Mindseye developer Build a Rocket Boy - the company created by former Rockstar and Grand Theft Auto producer Leslie Benzies - apparently owes approximately £62 million in debt. And a huge chunk of that appears to be owed to Chinese gaming company NetEase (£36.5m), though more than £1m appears to be owed to Benzies himself.

Recent findings suggest that this came to light in a proposal issued by Build a Rocket Boy's administrators this week (spotted by Resetera), which lists both the moneys owed (right down to a £20 charge to OpenAI) and details what went wrong, as well as what Build a Rocket Boy intends to do to recoup money to pay the debts back. And the tech giant's "largest" potential asset, according to the administrators, is litigation.

Industry observers note that "Prior to the Firm's entry into Administration, the directors had been investigating circumstances surrounding the commercial performance of the video game, MindsEye, which was released in 2025 following significant development investment," the administration proposal read. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary.

Sources indicate that "The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that any such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions.".

In a recent development, this tallies with the narrative spun by co-tech giant leader Mark Gerhard as the company waded into deep water. Gerhard blamed "organised espionage and corporate sabotage" for the studio's difficulties as multiple rounds of layoffs shredded Build a Rocket Boy. "People had their hands on the scale and deliberately tried to shape a negative narrative around the product," Gerhard said.

The situation he's referring to is likely the alleged smear campaign made against the game, which Gerhand reportedly claimed in an internal meeting this year was paid for by a "big American organization" and then run by a UK company called Ritual Network, which apparently had influencers, journalists and staff at Build a Rocket Boy deliberately sabotage the game's release. That's according to an account of a videoed internal meeting reportedly seen by Insider Gaming earlier this year.

It had nothing to do with the dire state of Mindseye when it launched, then. Eurogamer awarded it one out of five stars, chastising its "ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat" in our Mindseye review.

In a recent development, build a Rocket Boy was founded in 2016, and its first game, Everywhere - a sort of online gaming platform - was confirmed in 2022. It never materialised, but a part of that vision was carved out to become a standalone game experience of its own along the way, and that's how we got Mindseye - a take on a Grand Theft Auto formula. Whether or not the litigation is successful and can recoup any of Build a Rocket Boy's debts remains to be seen, but there's a financial mountain for the studio to climb if it hopes to operate again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream demonstrated off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of major ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more promptly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

Sources indicate that "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs noted, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

How to use NOS in GTA 6

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using GTA 6 NOS to give your car a boost can be helpful in street races and just for getting around, but the game doesn't make it very clear how it's used with some easy-to-miss prompts.
  • In a recent development, to use nitrous in GTA 6, you must hold L3/LS while fully pressing R2/RT.
  • Obviously, you must also be driving a GTA 6 car that has Nitrous Boost installed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Using GTA 6 NOS to give your car a boost can be helpful in street races and just for getting around, but the game doesn't make it very clear how it's used with some easy-to-miss prompts. In short, it's a bit like having a sprint for your car, so it's pretty simple to use, but I've explained how it all works in GTA 6 just below.

In a recent development, to use nitrous in GTA 6, you must hold L3/LS while fully pressing R2/RT. If you press in the left stick while at anything other than full throttle, you'll just honk your horn instead.

Obviously, you must also be driving a GTA 6 car that has Nitrous Boost installed. Any Mod Shop can install this component for you for $5,000, and it's found under the Performance tab, then the Boost section – depending on the car, it can also provide small boosts to its speed and acceleration stats. Otherwise, cars with NOS already installed are incredibly rare but there's a Declasse Yosemite 1500 called the Nutbusta that comes with nitrous that you can steal for Moses in Chapter 2, so you might want to keep that rather than sell it.

It has been revealed that you can tell a car has NOS installed because it'll have a blue ring icon next to the engine health and fuel gauges. You can only use your NOS boost in short bursts as the blue ring indicating how much nitrous you have will rapidly empty when using it. Conveniently it refills on its own unlike regular gas as you need to refuel your car in GTA 6.

Sources indicate that but bear in mind that, from my experience using the nitrous boost in GTA 6, the extra speed isn't that spectacular, with the camera field-of-view and zoom out making it feel faster than it actually is. It's certainly not unhelpful for street races, but don't expect it to surge you into first place.

And if you're wondering what car is in all the images in this article, it's the GTA 6 Paul Walker car – incredibly, it doesn't come with NOS as standard, but I had to fit it as soon as possible to make it just like the car in The Fast and the Furious.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that some Infinity Nikki fans are planning to boycott the game following the release of the game's latest trailer, which is narrated by Maye Musk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, cozy, open-world dress-up game, is at the centre of controversy again, though this time not because fans disliked one of the game's updates. Instead, it's because of… Elon Musk's mother.

Recent findings suggest that some Infinity Nikki fans are planning to boycott the game following the release of the game's latest trailer, which is narrated by Maye Musk. The trailer is for a latest update - dubbed Cicia - which adds the ability to drive futuristic hovering cars. The reveal comes days after a widely mocked demonstration of Musk's own Tesla "flying car", which doesn't actually fly.

While some fans are worried Tesla's cars may be coming to the game, many also simply don't want their game associated with Elon Musk and his family.

"If they promote Tesla or mention him in the game I'm 100 percent dropping it," wrote one Reddit user (via The Gamer). "Why would they involve that man in a girly fashion game, and if they wanted a car brand partnership why not a Chinese one??!? Infold is addicted to negative attention I swear.".

Recent findings suggest that "If Tesla is somehow involved in the design of the car (or worse, an in-game promotion), then I might have to let go," wrote another person in the same thread. "Please please please be wrong.".

Sources indicate that though Maye Musk's involvement might seem random, there may be a good explanation for it. "Here's something that might surprise people who only know her as Elon's mother: Maye Musk is a celebrity in China in her own right," Reddit user BarbieSpeedRacer explained.

"She's a successful model, an author, and a recognisable advertising personality. Her memoir became popular with Chinese readers, and she's appeared in campaigns and promotional events for brands including OPPO, Fila, and JNBY.".

Her image as "a woman in her seventies who continues to work as a fashion model" is one that resonates with the game's Chinese audience, apparently, especially "among women interested in fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content".

"A Chinese tech giant makes an advertisement featuring a celebrity popular in China, and an international fandom interprets that decision almost exclusively through the lens of American domestic politics," the post added.

Sources indicate that so far, calls for a boycott don't appear to have coalesced into a movement, at least judging by the game's subreddit. Even if Western players were to organise one, it's not likely to hurt Infinity Nikki much, as most of the game's revenue - estimated at more than 80 percent - comes from Chinese players.

In Eurogamer's Infinity Nikki review, Jessica Orr noted it advances the genre of open-world gacha games and brings competition to rival developer miHoYo, writing: "The changes in length, combat and progression all feel utterly invigorating compared to other Genshin-likes, and it's why Infinity Nikki feels like it could (and should) be on the same trajectory to shake up the gacha scene just like Genshin Impact did in 2020.".

Season 2 of Ace Combat Online begins on 1st December, 2026, and there's plenty of latest stuff for frequent flyers to enjoy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we think of secrecy surrounding movies, naturally we think MCU, but the amount of secrecy that went into The Odyssey is insane. While I knew everything about it was kept under wraps, I didn’t realize just how much until I heard John Leguizamo’s story about landing the script, and it’s WILD.

The actor portrays Odysseus's blind and devoted servant Eumaeus, a role that has been largely praised by critics. Turns out, Christopher Nolan knew exactly what he was doing when he cast Leguizamo in the part, and he didn’t even need to eat dessert first. The actor has previously gushed about working on the movie and the amazing shooting locations, but now he’s dishing to Kevin McCarthy on his On Film podcast about the Mission Impossible-level secret keeping that went into keeping the script under wraps:.

I would go to lunch at Odeon, his favorite restaurant. So we meet. He talks about the character. First of all, he talks about his career and everything. So that was just amazing to sit with him and hear him talk about his career was incredible. And then he states, ‘I have this role for you. It's one of the most loyal characters in Western literature.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that's a lot to live up to.’ He goes, ‘Yes.’ And I was like, ‘I'd love to do it if you'll have me.’ He offered me the role right there before dessert.

Recent findings suggest that leguizamo’s performance as Eumaeus has been called “sublime” by critics, and it’s easy to see why Nolan thought he was the right fit. Though the actor understands there’s a certain scene in the movie that earned him some hate for “the rest of cinema history,” and if you’ve seen it, then you know what he’s referring to. The actor didn’t even know the extent of his part until he got the script, which came to him as a top secret mission fit for James Bond:.

Sources indicate that A week later after we close the deal. I have to be home at 12:00 on a Tuesday to receive the script. Nobody else can receive it. I have to receive it. Sign for it. And it comes in a blood red color that you can only see, you know, during a full solstice. [laughter] I don't know. It's impossible to see, dude. The black ink is shiny, and the red makes it so you can't copy it. But it's hard to read. It's really difficult to read.

In a recent development, perhaps Marvel needs to take some notes from Nolan. While this seems like an insane level of secrecy for a book to screen adaptation, I admire the commitment to "no spoilers." Though the journalist asked the most vital question, who delivered the script? Surely, FedEx wasn’t tasked with such a feat. Turns out one of Nolan’s personal assistants hand delivered it. However, there was still another step for him to be able to keep the confidential script:.

That's given to me, and I'm not allowed to share with anybody. My assistant had to sign an NDA.

Sources indicate that the cloak and dagger seems to have worked as not even Tom Holland seems to have leaked anything. Additionally, Leguizamo shared that whenever Nolan made tweaks, the actor would have to turn in the old pages. This was definitely a first in his career, but one he feels was completely worth it, and I have to agree as the actor seemed to easily embody the role.

According to recent reports, it’s not easy to bring an epic of this scale to life, and it was clear from the get-go that Nolan had a vision. Now that The Odyssey hit the 2026 movie schedule over the summer, the actor can focus on a different role. Though maybe one that doesn’t come with as much secrecy? Leguizamo will reprising his role as Sid the sloth in the upcoming 2027 movie, Ice Age: Boiling Point, which is set for a February 5, 2027 release.

Someone should ask him if he was given the Ice Age 6 script in red. Regardless, I’d love to hear his co-stars take on the spy antics it took to keep the script out of the wrong hands.

#121374. Industry News: They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • Industry observers note that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

Industry observers note that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

Recent findings suggest that that means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Sources indicate that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

Industry observers note that while we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to upgrade the image. Like I noted, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

Sources indicate that I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

Industry observers note that the "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Industry observers note that pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

It has been revealed that for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

According to recent reports, after a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

Industry observers note that if that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

It has been revealed that indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

Industry observers note that however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot upcoming thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

Sources indicate that in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the latest PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Industry observers note that early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint concern in bright ambient light.

Recent findings suggest that if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Industry observers note that not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the newly introduced RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the upcoming 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of challenges like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The massive brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.
